Hi HN, I'm Cody, I have 847 YouTube playlists, and always hated that YouTube failed to provide basic playlist management tools. Ctrl+F was never convenient and breaks past 200 playlists. So I built & shipped my first Chrome extension. It replaces the Save dialog with a native-feeling searchable one that fetches all your playlists (and whether the current video is saved there) directly from YouTube's InnerTube API. It works robustly across every current save surface (watch page, home feed, search results, Shorts via right-click or Alt+S).
This version is faster and more stable than my original attempt. In 1.0 I read and wrote YouTube's DOM directly. It felt like the efficient approach, but makes for constant UI regressions as YouTube changes, so I can't recommend it. In 2.0 the UI lives outside YouTube's app tree in a closed shadow root, and the data comes from YouTube's internal InnerTube JSON API. The trigger it uses is a small hook wrapping the page's fetch, i.e. when YouTube's client requests the add-to-playlist panel.
Privacy: As private as possible given it's a YouTube extension. The extension only talks to youtube.com, doesn't ship any third-party code, and stores nothing about your playlists, just two display preferences: sort order, and the privacy new playlists are created with. AGPL-3.0.
Install:
https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/efgbkmnooapcpdpgmih...
Source:
https://github.com/codyhxyz/playlist-search-extension
Site:
https://playlist.codyh.xyz/
Bonus:
Technically you can replicate the filter-bar functionality with a dev console script, which I've linked here: (
https://gist.github.com/codyhxyz/00001e74d238ae5911ccfc8f8d4...
). For obvious reasons, I prefer a dedicated extension.
Happy to answer anything about my approach including the InnerTube API or about the shadow-root. Always looking to improve the extension's architecture.

A month ago, I shared mini-AGI, an experiment in training a byte-level, continually learning language model from scratch on a single 8 GB laptop GPU (an RTX 3070).
To recap the setup briefly: it completely decouples model size from VRAM by paging experts to and from an NVMe drive (currently 397 experts / 1.26B total parameters on disk, with only 32 resident / ~109M active in 5.1 GB of VRAM). It trains on a single stream at batch 1, with the attention/embedding trunk learning rate dampened to 0.1x to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
The training is still going and went only through ~35% of the training corpus selected at the beginning of the run (about 8GB in total). Here is the current status:
1. enwik9 (First 10^9 bytes of English Wikipedia):
Model               Params   Data Read       Cost     enwik9 (bits/byte) ↓
Llama-3.2-1B        1.23B    36 TB (9T tok)  ~$900k   0.68
Chinchilla 1B       1.00B    5.6 TB          ~$68k    0.90
GPT-2 XL            1.56B    40 GB           ~$43k    1.07
GPT-2 Large         0.77B    40 GB           ~$21k    1.12
mini-AGI (online)   1.26B    2.8 GB          ~$56     1.14
GPT-2 Medium        0.35B    40 GB           ~$10k    1.17
mini-AGI (dynamic)  1.26B    2.8 GB          ~$56     1.23
mini-AGI (frozen)   1.26B    2.8 GB          ~$56     1.29
GPT-2 Small         0.12B    40 GB           ~$3k     1.33
2. PG19 (100 Project Gutenberg books, 41 MB test split):
Model               Params   Trained On        Cost    PG19 (bits/byte) ↓
MambaByte-972M       0.97B   75 GB (PG19)      ~$4k    0.883
MegaByte-1B          1.02B   80 GB (PG19)      ~$1.6k  1.000
Transformer-320M     0.32B   80 GB (PG19)      ~$1.6k  1.057
mini-AGI (online)    1.26B   2.8 GB (0 PG19)   ~$56    1.447
mini-AGI (frozen)    1.26B   2.8 GB (0 PG19)   ~$56    1.995
The published models were trained on PG19's own training books, 75 to 80 GB of them, and are scored on more books like those. mini-AGI has never been trained on PG19 and has read no Victorian novels, so for it these books are completely out of its domain.
There are more details in the repository. The most important part is a difference between "frozen" and "online" attempts where we allow the model to specialize on the task as it goes through the evaluation dataset. Clearly showcasing the power of continual learning regime simply unavailable for any other typical LLM.

- [author] ppcvote: Hi HN. I run a one-person company in Taiwan. MindThread is a Threads scheduler with paying users here, and it already had a REST API. This release wraps it for agents: a CLI (`npx mindthread-cli`) and an MCP server (`npx -y mindthread-mcp`, or hosted at https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp , registry id io.github.ppcvote/mindthread). Your agent can draft posts in the account's voice, publish or schedule text, images, carousels and video, work a queue, read insights, and review reply drafts from "cloud patrol", which searches Threads for your keywords. Everything in this release goes through Meta's official Threads API, so no passwords. (A separate, Taiwan-only browser extension exists and is not part of this.) The part I care about most is control. Each key has allow, ask or deny per permission (publish now, schedule, send replies, turn on patrol). With ask, the call returns `approval_required` and a link, and nothing goes out until the owner confirms on mindthread.tw. In the CLI that is exit code 3, so the agent stops instead of retrying. Defaults for a new live key: publish now, sending replies, enabling patrol and loosening guardrails ask first; scheduling a post 30+ minutes ahead is allowed, and you can set it to ask. Content rules (length, banned phrases, only numbers from your fact list) are checked by the server on every API write and again at publish time. With `enforce: block` a violating post is refused; the default is `warn`, which only flags it. Limits: Threads only. - [author] ppcvote: Hi HN. I run a one-person company in Taiwan. MindThread is a Threads scheduler with paying users here, and it already had a REST API. This release wraps it for agents: a CLI (`npx mindthread-cli`) and an MCP server (`npx -y mindthread-mcp`, or hosted at https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp , registry id io.github.ppcvote/mindthread). Your agent can draft posts in the account's voice, publish or schedule text, images, carousels and video, work a queue, read insights, and review reply drafts from "cloud patrol", which searches Threads for your keywords. Everything in this release goes through Meta's official Threads API, so no passwords. (A separate, Taiwan-only browser extension exists and is not part of this.) The part I care about most is control. Each key has allow, ask or deny per permission (publish now, schedule, send replies, turn on patrol). With ask, the call returns `approval_required` and a link, and nothing goes out until the owner confirms on mindthread.tw. In the CLI that is exit code 3, so the agent stops instead of retrying. Defaults for a new live key: publish now, sending replies, enabling patrol and loosening guardrails ask first; scheduling a post 30+ minutes ahead is allowed, and you can set it to ask. Content rules (length, banned phrases, only numbers from your fact list) are checked by the server on every API write and again at publish time. With `enforce: block` a violating post is refused; the default is `warn`, which only flags it. Limits: Threads only. Free plan is 1 account, 3 posts a day and 50 calls a day per live key, and Meta's per-profile caps apply on top. The MCP server lacks the thread, webhook and A/B tools the CLI has. The CLI and bridge are MIT; the service is hosted. No signup needed to look around: `curl https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp ` lists the tools, and `tools/list`, `get_playbook` and `list_formulas` work without a key. A free account gives you a `mt_test_` sandbox key. A `mt_test_` key simulates every write. Feedback I want: is per-permission ask the right granularity, and what would you need before letting an agent post for you?

- [author] ppcvote: Hi HN. I run a one-person company in Taiwan. MindThread is a Threads scheduler with paying users here, and it already had a REST API. This release wraps it for agents: a CLI (`npx mindthread-cli`) and an MCP server (`npx -y mindthread-mcp`, or hosted at https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp , registry id io.github.ppcvote/mindthread). Your agent can draft posts in the account's voice, publish or schedule text, images, carousels and video, work a queue, read insights, and review reply drafts from "cloud patrol", which searches Threads for your keywords. Everything in this release goes through Meta's official Threads API, so no passwords. (A separate, Taiwan-only browser extension exists and is not part of this.) The part I care about most is control. Each key has allow, ask or deny per permission (publish now, schedule, send replies, turn on patrol). With ask, the call returns `approval_required` and a link, and nothing goes out until the owner confirms on mindthread.tw. In the CLI that is exit code 3, so the agent stops instead of retrying. internal projects use tagged plugin versions and run records to capture the plugin version, configuration, and starting code revision. These records help engineers trace unexpected results to a specific version or configuration, while
code review
and repeatable evaluations help teams assess AI behavior before proceeding.

The clinical education platform records each AI call’s provider and model, response time, status, retry attempts, errors, token usage, and content. It also captures the reason a call finished. These records help engineers investigate unexpected model behavior and trace individual requests. If performance signals change, they can compare results against the evaluation baseline and rerun relevant tests before approving a prompt, model, or configuration change.

healthcare software
, similar traceability can help teams review how an AI-assisted feature handled clinical information or generated a result, where those records are captured by the system. projects use evaluation reports and run ledgers to track task progress, review outcomes, model behavior, and costs. The records also capture the plugin version, workflow configuration, and starting code revision, which helps engineers trace a run to the setup under which it began.

Missing fields can suggest an extraction problem, while slower responses or rising costs may follow a model or configuration change. Teams can use these findings to investigate and rerun evaluations.
Audit needs depend on the feature. An AI-generated clinical examination score may require records of the model and output for later review, while storing raw user content can create unnecessary exposure elsewhere. Keeping relevant records helps teams investigate failures and explain how a system produced a result.
How GeekyAnts Manages AI Data Retention, Provider Selection, and Hosting
Before adding an AI feature, teams need to know what data it sends to a provider, what stays in the application, and how long records remain available. Retention requirements depend on the feature and project; one rule does not fit every workflow.

A clear account of data flows, retention, and available provider options gives clients a basis for making informed decisions before starting the implementation process.

ghcr.io/gowthamgts/mailrelay:latest

SMTP ──▶ SPF / DKIM / DMARC ──▶ rule matching ──▶ webhooks (async, with retries)
(off | log | enforce)          every matching rule fires
